project: quay-krewe: a project carries its own context
rewritten: 2026-09-05, a fifth time, after the operator settled the four levels

user_actions.1: A project holds a brief and a design, and any write to the design clears the approval.
user_actions.2: The design carries a numbered path of atomised changes.
user_actions.3: The operator takes a step, and the session proves it understood before it builds. Several steps run at once, up to the project's cap, and a take is refused when two steps name the same file.
user_actions.4: The operator approves a restatement, and the session builds.
user_actions.5: The operator reads the state of the path.
user_actions.6: Krewe checks the proof, and a step records what came of it.
user_actions.7: Krewe earns the word done, and can lose it.
user_actions.8: The operator drives krewe from a slash command in their own session. Krewe writes those command files, and an install never writes over a file somebody else wrote.
user_actions.9: A project holds features, and each feature is delivered in milestones. A step belongs to one milestone, and it names the contracts it builds.
user_actions.10: The operator archives a finished session. The listing hides it and keeps its record, and the last line says how many are hidden.

rules: One intention per slice. One reviewable pull request per slice. Revertable alone.
Every slice ships its scenarios in the same change. The promises gate refuses a behaviour change that carries no scenario.
Each slice is written for somebody who was not in the design conversation.
S-5 is the gate. If the measurement says no, every slice after it is cancelled.

The whole suite runs on this machine and in continuous integration. It takes about 42 seconds and peaks at about 1.18 gigabytes. The local gates are make test, go build, go vet, gofmt and golangci-lint.
Each slice names the milestone of .greenlight/ROADMAP.md it belongs to. Twenty two milestones, forty four slices, because a milestone that is more than one reviewable pull request is split.

The dependency edges order by meaning, not by file. Section 5.1 of the design measures what that does not record. From milestone 7 on, several steps may be taken at once, capped at three by default, and every take is a command the operator typed.

Identifiers never move. S-36 to S-43 came after S-35 and were placed in the order through depends_on, because merged pull requests name the earlier ones. S-44 came after those and depends on nothing. Order comes from the graph, never from the number.

slices.changes: TakeStep splits the touches text on newlines. It reads the step being taken and every step in state taken in the whole project, across every feature. It trims the spaces at each end and drops empty lines. It refuses an exact match, naming the first collision in step number order. SetPath warns about a step naming no file.
slices.proves: features/path.feature. Taking a step naming internal/store/store.go while a taken step names it is refused, naming the file and that step. A step of feature 2 naming a file that a taken step of feature 1 names is refused, and the refusal names feature 1. The next step of feature 2, naming a different file, is taken while the first one waits. Two steps naming different files are both taken. A file written with trailing spaces still collides. A step naming no file is taken, and setting that path warned.
slices.risk: The check reads what a step says it writes, never a diff. A step that writes a file it did not name is not caught. Section 14 of the design defers the diff based check, and FLIGHT-3 records the limit. A sequential number is not a filename either, so two steps that each add a migration take the same number and both takes pass. Section 5.1 of the design measures that and section 14 defers the fix.
slices.note: The query is by project, across every feature, and never by feature. A feature must not collide with another feature, the same way a step must not collide with another step. It is one rule at one level. The refusal lands on the step, never on the feature, so a feature waits on one step and carries on with the rest. The check lives in the store, in the same statement as the take. A read in the control plane, then a write, would let two takes pass at the same moment.

slices.proves: features/path.feature. At level 1, a passing check closes the step and names krewe as the closer. A failing check closes nothing. At level 0, a passing check closes nothing.
slices.note: A failing check closes nothing at any level. That is the one rule the ladder never bends.

slices.name: The operator reopens a step krewe closed
slices.intention: Give the operator a way to correct krewe, and make the correction cost the level.
slices.changes: One store method, one remote procedure call, and the word krewe step reopen. A reopen sets the step back to taken, records a disagreement, lowers the level by one and sets the run to zero.
slices.proves: features/path.feature. A reopen of a step krewe closed lowers the level and restarts the run. A reopen of a step the operator closed is refused. The reopened step is taken again, by the same session.
slices.note: The level falls by one, never to zero from any height. No measurement supports a bigger fall. Nothing restarts and nothing dispatches.

slices.name: A skill teaches a session to design a project
slices.intention: Let an ordinary session carry the ideation and the design, with no machinery around it.
slices.changes: One skill, prose only, no code. It tells a session to read the brief and the repository, and then to write the design. It tells it to write the path in the grammar, and to name a scenario on every step. It tells it never to approve. It states the six parts of a restatement.
slices.proves: features/design.feature. A session dispatched with the skill writes a design and a path that read back whole. Every step names a scenario. The design it wrote is not approved.
slices.note: This is the headline capability and it rests on everything above it. The session stays ordinary and is dispatched by hand. No controller and no gate on it.

slices.name: The console draws a project's path
slices.intention: Let the operator read the path without leaving the console.
slices.changes: A path resource, drilled into from a project. Columns: number, title, state, proof, closed by, session, age. A step that waits for the operator draws waiting on you. Enter descends into the project's sessions when the step names one.
slices.proves: internal/console table tests for the columns, the order, the derived cell and the refusal. features/console.feature for the view opening by name.
slices.note: SortBy is -1. The control plane answers in number order, and sorting rendered text would put step 10 above step 2. It depends on S-25 because the closer cell reads a column that migration 0069 adds.

slices.name: The project row counts the steps, the trust level and the flight
slices.intention: Say how far a project got, and where krewe stands, on the listing an operator already reads.
slices.changes: The projects view gains two cells. One counts done steps out of total. The other shows the trust level with the run behind it, and says when an offer stands. One ListSteps call per draw, not one per project.
slices.proves: internal/console table tests. A project with seven steps, three done, draws 3/7. A project with no path draws an empty cell. A project at level 0 with two agreements draws 0 (2/5). A project with a standing offer says so.
slices.note: Project gains no field on the wire. Both cells are derived by the reader.

slices.name: Krewe installs the slash commands, and the init command ships
slices.intention: Put krewe in the operator's own terminal, and prove an install never writes over somebody else's file.

partial_contracts.SLASH-1: The embed, the marker and the file format. The set holds one file here, and grows to four.
partial_contracts.SLASH-3: Whole, as a test over the embedded set. It runs again on every file a later slice adds.
partial_contracts.COMMAND-23: The listing. It names one command here, and four after S-35.

slices.changes: A new commands directory carrying one markdown file. A new internal package holding the embed and the install. The words krewe commands, krewe commands install and krewe commands list. Nothing touches the store.
slices.proves: features/commands.feature. An install writes every file and names where each went. A second install replaces the files krewe wrote. An install over a file with no marker refuses, names it, and writes nothing at all. Every embedded file carries the marker on line one. Every verb the files name appears in the manual.
slices.gate: There is no flag that forces a write over an unmarked file. One scenario reads the flag table and proves none exists.
slices.why_here: The install mechanism alone could ship after S-3. It waits because milestone 15 ships the design command beside it, and that command dispatches a session holding the skill of S-29.
slices.note: No migration, no table, no protobuf message and no remote procedure call. A reader who expects one should stop looking.

slices.name: The design command asks, dispatches, and shows the design back
slices.intention: Let the operator run the whole design conversation from their own terminal.
slices.changes: One markdown file. It asks the design questions in the operator's session. It then dispatches a krewe session that holds the design skill. It reads the body back with krewe design, and runs krewe design approve on a yes.
slices.proves: features/commands.feature. The file installs and carries the marker. It names only verbs the manual carries. It writes no design body itself. Answering no leaves the design unapproved.
slices.risk: This is the command where breaking the rule of SLASH-3 would be easiest. A scenario reads the file and refuses a design body written in the operator's session.
slices.note: The design work stays in a krewe session in a sandbox, where the record keeps it.

slices.name: The status command prints one readout of the path
slices.intention: Give the operator the whole state of a project in one line of typing.
slices.changes: One markdown file. It runs krewe path, krewe sessions and krewe design. It prints the steps in flight against the cap, what waits on the operator, the next step and the trust level.
slices.proves: features/commands.feature. The file installs and carries the marker. It names only verbs the manual carries. A project with two steps in flight and a cap of three reads back as such. A project with no path names the command that writes one.
slices.why_here: It reads the cap from S-14, the next step from S-13 and the trust level from S-25. All three are ancestors of S-32, so the only edge it needs is the install.
slices.note: It writes nothing. Every number in the readout comes from a row somebody else wrote.

slices.name: The trust command prints the ladder and raises it on a yes
slices.intention: Put the offer in front of the operator where they already stand.

partial_contracts.COMMAND-23: The listing now names four commands, in the order init, design, status, trust.

slices.changes: One markdown file. It runs krewe trust, prints the level, the run, the threshold and any standing offer, and runs krewe trust raise on a yes. The listing now names four commands.
slices.proves: features/commands.feature. The file installs and carries the marker. With an offer standing, a yes raises the level and krewe trust then says level 1. With no offer it prints the run and asks nothing. Answering no leaves the level where it was.
slices.note: It never lowers a level. A wrong close does that, through krewe step reopen.

slices.name: A project holds features
slices.intention: Give a project somewhere to keep each narrowed part of itself.

partial_contracts.TABLE-3: The columns migration 0065 creates, including state. The verbs that write state come in S-39.
partial_contracts.LEVEL-1: The feature level only. The milestone level comes in S-38. The step key moves in S-37.

slices.changes: A third table, three store methods, a Feature message and three remote procedure calls. The words krewe feature, krewe feature add and krewe feature intention. Nothing about the path changes yet, so every step still hangs off its project.
slices.proves: features/path.feature. Adding two features to a project gives them the numbers 1 and 2. A second project starts again at 1. A feature with an empty title is refused. Reading a project with no feature says so and names the command that adds one.
slices.note: The server gives the number, never the caller, so two adds at one moment cannot take the same one. The read of the highest number and the insert are one statement.

slices.name: A path belongs to a feature
slices.intention: Move the key of the step table from the project to the feature, before anything else is built on the old key.

partial_contracts.TABLE-2: What migration 0066 changes. The milestone column comes in S-38, the contracts columns in S-43.
partial_contracts.LEVEL-2: The whole substitution, and the refusal that meets a bare step number.
partial_contracts.STORE-5: The feature key, and the rule that another feature is untouched. The milestones come in S-38.
partial_contracts.COMMAND-7: The feature number and the whole feature listing. The milestone grouping comes in S-40.
partial_contracts.WIRE-8: The feature field. The milestones field comes in S-38.

slices.changes: Migration 0066 renames project_steps to feature_steps, adds feature, drops project, and moves the primary key. It adds one feature for every project that already holds steps, and points those steps at it. Every store method, request message and command that reached a step through a project reaches it through a feature. A step is typed as one token, feature.number. Every read of steps in flight is scoped to the project and never to the feature.
slices.proves: features/path.feature. Setting the path of feature 2 leaves the path of feature 1 whole. Two features each hold a step 3, and taking one leaves the other ready. A bare step number is refused, and the refusal names the form and the features that exist. Steps written before the migration read back under one feature, with every column kept.
slices.why_here: Twenty six slices ahead of this one assumed the step table was keyed by the project. Re-keying now costs one migration and an amendment to three merged slices, S-8, S-9 and S-10. Re-keying at slice thirty costs the same migration plus every slice built on the old key.
slices.risk: The up migration writes rows, not only a schema. A project that holds steps gets a feature it did not ask for, titled with the project name. The down migration cannot reverse a feature the operator added afterwards, and it says so in its own comment. The second risk is a query. Once the step table is keyed by the feature, the natural read is steps in flight in this feature, and that read lets two features write one file at the same moment. Every count of steps in flight is by project, across every feature. S-14 and S-15 build those reads, and STORE-8 states the rule.

slices.name: A feature is delivered in milestones
slices.intention: Group the steps of a feature, so a reader sees what a run of steps adds up to.

partial_contracts.TABLE-2: The milestone column that migration 0067 adds.
partial_contracts.GRAMMAR-1: The milestone heading, its intention line, and every milestone refusal. The contract labels come in S-43.
partial_contracts.STORE-5: The milestones written in the same transaction as the steps.
partial_contracts.WIRE-8: The milestones field on the response.
partial_contracts.LEVEL-1: The milestone level, which completes the contract.

slices.changes: A fourth table, one store method, a Milestone message, and a milestone column on the step table. The path document gains a heading above the steps, reading # 4. A design carries a numbered path, with one line under it. SetPath writes the milestones and the steps from that one document, in one transaction.
slices.proves: features/path.feature. A document with three milestone headings writes three milestone rows, and each step carries the number of the milestone above it. A document with no milestone heading gives every step a milestone of 0. Two steps numbered 1 under different milestones are refused, naming both lines. A document opening with a hash line that carries no number parses, and that line is ignored.
slices.note: Step numbers are unique across the feature, not inside a milestone. That is the trap in this grammar, because a reader expects the numbering to start again under each milestone. The refusal says so in those words.

slices.name: The operator closes a feature
slices.intention: Let the operator say a feature finished, so the record of the work stops growing.

partial_contracts.TABLE-3: The writes to state, which complete the table's contract.

slices.changes: One store method, one remote procedure call, and the words krewe feature done, krewe feature stop and krewe feature open. Closing a feature warns about each step under it that is not finished, and it does not refuse. The operator decides when a feature is finished.
slices.proves: features/path.feature. Closing a feature with a taken step prints a warning naming that step, and closes it anyway. A state word outside the three is refused, naming the three. The steps of a closed feature read back unchanged. Reopening a closed feature writes the word open.
slices.why_before_s41: S-41 leaves a closed feature out of the path document a session reads. Without these verbs nothing can close a feature, so no scenario can prove that rule.

slices.name: The path listing groups the steps under their milestones
slices.intention: Let the operator read where the feature reached, without counting rows by hand.

partial_contracts.COMMAND-7: The milestone grouping, the count on each heading, and the count under the list. The feature number and the whole feature listing shipped in S-37.

slices.changes: krewe path prints each milestone as a heading carrying its number, its title and a count reading so many steps and so many done. The steps print under it, in number order. One line under the whole list counts the steps of the feature by state, and one line says which step is next.
slices.proves: features/path.feature. A path of five steps under two milestones prints two headings, five step lines and a count. Each heading carries the count of its own steps and how many are done. A step whose milestone is 0 prints under the heading no milestone. With no feature number, two open features print two headings and a closed third one is left out.
slices.note: This answers the question the operator asked of the tool: where is this project. Before it, the honest answer was that somebody reads the git log.

slices.name: The path document a session reads names each step's milestone
slices.intention: Let a session see which milestone its step belongs to, and what the steps around it reached.

partial_contracts.RENDER-3: The feature heading, the milestone heading, the milestone line in each block, and the rule that a closed feature is left out. The state line shipped in S-9, the result line in S-12 and the proof line in S-20.

slices.changes: Every render writes .krewe/path.md with one heading per open feature, one heading per milestone, and one block per step. Each block names its milestone, so a reader who opens the file at one step still knows where the step sits. A feature that is done or stopped is left out.
slices.proves: features/path.feature. A session dispatched into a project with two open features reads both in .krewe/path.md, each under its own heading. Each step block names its milestone. Closing a feature takes it out of the file on the next dispatch. Reopening it brings it back.
slices.note: Leaving a closed feature out is what keeps this file from growing with every finished feature. A session opens it on demand, so the cost is a read and not context.

slices.name: A project carries a contracts document
slices.intention: Give a session the contracts to build against, in a file it opens rather than in the memory file it always pays for.

partial_contracts.TABLE-1: The contracts column that migration 0068 adds.
partial_contracts.WIRE-1: The contracts field on the Design message.

slices.changes: One column on the design row, one store method, one remote procedure call, and the word krewe design contracts. Every render writes .krewe/contracts.md into the session's working directory, exactly as it writes .krewe/design.md.
slices.proves: features/design.feature. A session dispatched into a project with a contracts document finds it whole at .krewe/contracts.md. Setting the contracts document on an approved design leaves the design approved. A project with no contracts document has no such file.
slices.note: Writing the contracts document does not clear the approval. The approval is the operator's word about the design body, and the contracts document is read from that body. This project carries 127 contracts across 44 slices, which is why it is a file the model opens and not text in a memory file.

slices.name: A step names the contracts it builds
slices.intention: Carry the scoping the operator writes by hand today, so the take text says which part of a contract is this step's.

partial_contracts.TABLE-2: The contracts and contract_scope columns that migration 0069 adds, which complete the table.
partial_contracts.GRAMMAR-1: The two contract labels and their refusals, which complete the grammar.
partial_contracts.RENDER-4: The two contract blocks and the pointer to .krewe/contracts.md. The step body shipped in S-10, and S-16 replaces the tail.

slices.changes: Two columns on the step table, two labels in the path document, and two blocks in the take text. A step names the contracts it builds, one identifier per line. It names the scope of each, one line per contract, saying which part is this step's and which part waits for a later step.
slices.proves: features/path.feature. A document naming two contracts and two scopes reads back on the step. A scope line naming a contract the step does not build is refused, naming the line. Taking that step dispatches a session whose text names both contracts, both scopes, and the contracts document. A step with no contracts produces text with no contracts label in it.
slices.note: Every step brief this project wrote by hand carried this scoping, copied out of the graph. The one time a contract was wrong, a session refused to build and asked, which cost a slice of work. Nothing checks that a named contract exists in the contracts document, and the deferred list in the design records that.

slices.name: A session is archived, and the listing hides it
slices.intention: Keep the record of every session, and stop the finished ones from burying the live ones.
slices.changes: The words krewe archive and krewe unarchive, and the flag --archived on krewe sessions. One store method, ArchiveProjectSessions, and one widened one, ArchiveSession. One new call on the wire, and a hidden count on the session listing response. No migration and no column: archived_at exists already, from migration 0004_archive_sessions, and this slice reads it. ArchiveSession loses one behaviour and gains one refusal: it stops a session of any status today, and it refuses a session that holds an open exec from here on.
slices.proves: features/sessions.feature. Archiving a stopped session takes it out of the default listing and leaves its conversation, its exec history and its files where they are. The listing then says how many are hidden and names the flag that shows them. krewe sessions --archived lists the archived ones and never mixes the two. Archiving a project archives every session that holds no container, and says how many it left. Archiving a session that holds an open exec is refused, and the refusal names the exec. The console key shows the same refusal, which is the way off the old behaviour. Unarchiving puts a session back, reading stopped, and the next exec builds a fresh container.
slices.why_here: It depends on nothing. The sessions table, the archive stamp and the session listing all exist today, so this slice can be built at any point in the path. It is placed last because it answers a different question from milestones 1 to 21, which are one design and one path.
slices.note: It is independent by dependency and not by file. Measured on the graph of 44 slices on 2026-09-05, it shares at least one file with 34 of the other 43 slices, and with seven of the eight from S-36 to S-43. S-40 is the one exception, because it touches only cmd/krewe/path.go, internal/controlplane/design.go and the path feature files. So the file collision check of FLIGHT-3 refuses to take this step beside almost any other. Take it alone, or take it beside S-40. Nothing here is partial, so this slice carries no partial_contracts: TABLE-5 states a column that exists, and no later slice widens any of the nine.
